headline: 75.5% on time across 635,459 flights
problem: US DOT publishes a year of Florida departures as 6.5 million raw rows with 109 columns. Travellers and operators want plain answers: which airports, airlines and hours run late, and why.
contribution: Solo project. I built the star schema (635,459 flights, four dimensions), the DAX measures with a whole-Florida benchmark, the Power BI report, and a pandas script that recomputes every card to test it.
result: Time of day matters about twice as much as the airline; late-arriving aircraft cause 42.5% of delay minutes. The web preview here is built from the same model; the .pbix is in the repo.
caption: The report page: KPI cards, on-time rate by month and departure hour, airlines ranked, delay causes, and the airport table.

screen.alt: A boarding pass printed with 75.5% on time across 635,459 flights.

sheet.alt: The Power BI report page: KPI cards, on-time rate by month and hour, airlines ranked, delay causes.

headline: 31 data tests over 1.07 million invoice lines
problem: Raw sales exports are never analysis-ready: duplicate rows, postage mixed with products, cancellations hiding inside sales. Every analyst cleans the file again, differently.
contribution: Solo project. I wrote staging, intermediate and mart layers in dbt on DuckDB, a seed of business rules, 31 data tests (five written for this data) and the generated lineage docs.
result: Net sales £18.18M after £1.46M of cancellations; champions are 25.1% of customers and 70.8% of revenue. Runs on demand on a laptop: no scheduler, CI or warehouse.
caption: A mart built by the pipeline: monthly product sales, net plus cancelled equals gross (December 2011 has only nine days of data). The lineage graph and data tests are in the case study.

screen.alt: A till receipt reading 31 of 31 data tests passed and net sales of 18.18 million pounds.

sheet.alt: Monthly product sales from the pipeline: net plus cancelled equals gross.

headline: 1.81% MAPE in rolling-origin backtests
problem: Monthly US retail sales swing hard with the calendar. A forecast has to get the seasonal shape right, and it is only worth something if you know how wrong it tends to be.
contribution: Solo project. I built the pipeline on Census data from 1992 onward: seasonal indices, five methods, a rolling-origin backtest, and ranges calibrated on the backtest's real errors.
result: The ETS + SARIMA average had 35% smaller backtest errors than 'same month last year'. Backtest accuracy, not a promise about future months; the calibrated 80% range is about 40% narrower than the models' own.
caption: The next 12 months: actual monthly sales, the ETS + SARIMA forecast, and the 80% range calibrated on the backtest.

screen.alt: A ruler marking a backtest error of 1.81% on a 0 to 10% scale.

sheet.alt: The next twelve months: actual sales, the ETS + SARIMA forecast and the calibrated 80% range.

headline: 20/20 figures within 0.5% of XBRL, 5/5 refusals
problem: A 10-K runs to hundreds of pages, and a fluent wrong number is worse than no answer. Can an LLM answer only from the filings, cite the passage, and admit when the answer is not there?
contribution: Solo project. I parsed five companies' latest 10-Ks from SEC EDGAR into 730 passages, compared keyword, embedding and hybrid search, and graded 30 questions against XBRL figures the model never sees.
result: Every money answer landed within 0.5% of XBRL with the figure in the cited passage; $0.10 for all 30 questions. The demo replays recorded answers; this site never calls an API.
